nameStory: The 'scarlet pimpernel' gets its name from those brilliant red flowers that seem to glow against the ground. The word 'pimpernel' traces back through French to Latin, originally meaning 'little pepper' - perhaps because the tiny seeds were once thought to be spicy. It's also called 'poor man's weather-glass' because the flowers famously close up when bad weather approaches!
description: Scarlet pimpernel is a low-growing annual plant that spreads along the ground like a colorful carpet. This European native produces tiny but incredibly bright flowers - usually vivid scarlet red, but sometimes brilliant blue or pink - that seem almost jewel-like against its small, oval leaves. The whole plant stays close to the earth, rarely rising more than a few inches tall, but can spread outward to form patches. It's considered a common weed that pops up in disturbed soils and sunny spots.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny but incredibly vibrant flowers, usually brilliant scarlet red (sometimes blue or pink), with 5 rounded petals that form perfect little stars. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch across but the color is so intense it catches your eye immediately.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stays very low to the ground, spreading horizontally rather than growing upward. The stems trail along the soil surface, creating small mats or patches that hug the earth.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, smooth, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. The leaves are bright green and feel soft to the touch, with no teeth or lobes along the edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers close up tight in cloudy weather or late afternoon, then reopen in bright sunshine. This weather-responsive behavior is so reliable that farmers once used it to predict rain!

habitat: Look for scarlet pimpernel in disturbed, sunny spots with light, sandy soils - roadsides, garden edges, vacant lots, and beach areas are prime territory. It thrives in places where the soil has been turned over or compacted, making it a common sight around construction sites and parking lot edges. While it prefers sandy or gravelly ground, this opportunistic plant will also pop up in heavier clay soils if the conditions are right.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin spreading their trailing stems along the ground. Early flowers may appear by late spring in sunny, warm spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when those brilliant scarlet (or blue) flowers are most abundant and noticeable. Flowers open wide in morning sunshine and close by late afternoon or in cloudy weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall until frost kills this annual plant. Seeds mature and scatter, ensuring next year's crop of colorful ground-huggers.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground growth - this annual dies completely with frost, surviving only as seeds in the soil waiting for warm spring weather.

funFact: Scarlet pimpernel flowers are so sensitive to atmospheric pressure that they close 2-3 hours before rain arrives - more reliable than many weather forecasts! This amazing ability earned it the nickname 'poor man's weather-glass' because people without barometers could predict storms just by watching these tiny flowers.
confusionNotes: The blue-flowered form is sometimes mistaken for a completely different plant, but it's the same species - just a color variation. The key is that low-growing, trailing habit and those perfectly formed 5-petaled star flowers, regardless of color.
contextualKnowledge: This little plant became famous as the emblem of the fictional hero 'The Scarlet Pimpernel' in Baroness Orczy's novels - chosen because like the elusive hero, the flower appears to vanish (closes up) when conditions become threatening. Despite being a European native, it's now found on every continent except Antarctica.
compareHints: Unlike its loosestrife cousins in the same genus, scarlet pimpernel stays ground-hugging rather than growing upright, and its flowers are much smaller but more intensely colored. While northern starflower also has small white star-shaped flowers, scarlet pimpernel's blooms are brilliantly red or blue and the plant has that distinctive trailing, mat-forming growth habit. Most other Lysimachia species grow as upright perennials, making scarlet pimpernel the odd one out as a prostrate annual.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its loosestrife relatives that tend to be taller with yellow flowers and different leaf arrangements, northern starflower is much shorter with its distinctive white seven-petaled blooms and single whorl of leaves.
Among New England's many Lysimachia species, whorled loosestrife is instantly recognizable by its four-leaf whorls - no other loosestrife has this arrangement.
Among its loosestrife relatives, swamp candles is unique for its tall, narrow flower spike - most other Lysimachia species have flowers in leaf axils or shorter, broader clusters.
Among New England's loosestrifes, fringed loosestrife is distinctive for its opposite leaves with fringed leaf stems and nodding yellow flowers.
Among its loosestrife relatives in New England, creeping Jenny is unique for its trailing, mat-forming habit - most other Lysimachia species stand upright.
Dotted loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife cousins mainly by those telltale petal spots - no other Lysimachia species has them.
Among the loosestrife family in New England, gooseneck loosestrife is the only one with the distinctive curved white flower spikes.
Unlike its loosestrife relatives that are mostly freshwater plants with showy yellow or white flowers, sea milkwort is the oddball of the family - adapted for salt water and lacking petals entirely.

Yellow loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife relatives by its tall stature and dense yellow flower clusters - most other Lysimachia species in New England are shorter with more scattered flowers.
Among its loosestrife cousins, tufted loosestrife is unique for having flowers that emerge from the sides of the stem rather than at the tips.

Among New England's yellow-flowered loosestrifes, lowland loosestrife is distinguished by its flowers tucked into leaf axils rather than arranged in showy spikes like swamp candles, or whorled around the stem like whorled loosestrife.
Among its loosestrife relatives, lanceleaf loosestrife is distinguished by its alternate (not opposite or whorled) leaf arrangement and narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Unlike its flashy cousin creeping Jenny (regular moneywort), miniature moneywort is truly miniature in every way - much smaller leaves, tinier flowers, and more delicate growth.

Unlike other Lysimachia species in New England that tend to be taller perennials with yellow flowers (like whorled loosestrife or swamp candles), blue scarlet pimpernel is a tiny blue-flowered annual that creeps along the ground.
